paragraphs: This paper examines how reliably recognition models handle deliberately altered 3D point clouds. Its starting finding concerns adversarial training, a leading defense: in the studied setting, it can obscure gradients rather than provide robustness against powerful attacks. This distinction matters because difficulty finding an attack does not necessarily mean that a model can withstand one.

The authors propose PointDP, which uses diffusion models to purify point clouds as a defense. Its training does not depend on a predefined collection of adversarial examples. This gives the method a way to address varied threats without tying its defense to that particular collection of attacks.

The evaluation covers six representative point cloud architectures and sixteen strong and adaptive attacks. Under strong attacks constrained by different ℓp norms, the authors report adversarial robustness improvements of 12.6%–40.3% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support diffusion-based purification across the evaluated architectures and threats, while the gradient-obfuscation finding explains why demanding attack evaluations are central to assessing the result.
icml-2023-a-critical-revisit-of-adversar.tldr: PointDP uses diffusion-based purification to improve 3D point cloud robustness against strong attacks while exposing weaknesses in adversarial training.

paragraphs: Learning to simulate physical systems from coarse data requires recovering details that downsampling removes. This paper shows that low-resolution features can lose substantial information, creating a problem for neural solvers of nonlinear partial differential equations. The issue is especially relevant when a model must preserve the evolving dynamics of a much finer simulation.

Temporal Stencil Modeling combines time-series sequence modeling through HiPPO features with learnable stencil modeling in neural PDE solvers. The approach aims to recover information from the trajectory over time. The authors describe it as a temporal extension of classical finite-volume methods such as WENO, connecting sequence modeling with an established numerical simulation framework.

For two-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes turbulence, TSM improves the duration of highly correlated simulation by 19.9% over the previously reported best result, while bringing inference latency to 80% of the comparison level. Experiments also show generalization to other turbulent-flow conditions, lower resolutions, and one- and three-dimensional settings. Together, these results support using temporal information to improve both simulation fidelity and execution speed.
icml-2023-a-neural-pde-solver-with-tempo.tldr: Temporal Stencil Modeling uses trajectory information to improve neural PDE simulation accuracy and reduce inference latency.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Social Rearrangement, a simulated setting where two robots cooperate on extended household tasks such as arranging a table or unpacking groceries. Each robot relies on onboard sensing and its own viewpoint, without privileged environmental information. The central challenge is coordinating with a new partner without first training together.

The authors find that earlier zero-shot coordination approaches struggle in this visually rich setting. Their analysis identifies insufficient variety in training-time coordination behaviors as a cause. Behavior Diversity Play addresses this through a discriminability objective that encourages distinguishable behaviors, giving training a stronger emphasis on diversity in how agents cooperate.

The resulting agents adapt to new partners in previously unseen environments. In the reported comparisons, BDP achieves 35% higher success and 32% higher efficiency than baselines. The findings connect training-time behavioral diversity with better coordination under unfamiliar partnerships. Although the task is motivated by robots working with new human partners, the reported setting involves cooperation between two simulated robots.
icml-2023-adaptive-coordination-in-socia.tldr: Encouraging diverse coordination behaviors helps simulated robots cooperate with unfamiliar partners in unseen environments.

paragraphs: Convolution works naturally on regularly arranged data, but graph nodes have an irregular structure and no inherent input ordering. The paper argues that existing graph convolutions struggle to learn diverse operators with limited parameters and often need separate mechanisms for extracting features at multiple scales. Its approach begins by changing how the graph is arranged.

The authors introduce a differentiable permutation method that places graph nodes into a row regardless of their original order. This arrangement supports a more flexible transfer of ordinary convolution to graphs. Their Compressed Convolution Network builds hierarchical representations using local feature learning and parameters shared throughout the model, following core mechanisms of convolutional neural networks.

CoCN is trained end to end and learns both node features and associated structural features. Tests on node-classification and graph-classification benchmarks show better performance than competitive convolutional graph networks and graph-pooling models. The result suggests that learning a useful arrangement of an irregular graph can support effective hierarchical feature extraction within a unified architecture.
icml-2023-all-in-a-row-compressed-convol.tldr: CoCN learns to arrange graph nodes into a row so convolution can build effective hierarchical graph representations.

paragraphs: This paper studies why Transformers can learn useful mappings between sequences even when the mathematical input and output spaces are infinite dimensional. It examines both approximation ability, meaning what the architecture can represent, and estimation ability, meaning how well a target can be learned. The goal is a theoretical account of performance on high-dimensional data.

The main result assumes anisotropic smoothness: the target function has different degrees of smoothness across its input directions. Under this structure, the authors show that feature extraction and parameter sharing allow Transformers to avoid the curse of dimensionality. The conclusion therefore depends on properties of the target function, rather than covering every possible infinite-dimensional mapping.

The analysis also allows smoothness to vary with the particular input. Transformers can then assess feature importance separately for each input and dynamically extract useful features. The authors prove convergence rates similar to those for fixed smoothness. This extends the explanation from a single fixed pattern of useful features to input-dependent feature selection.
icml-2023-approximation-and-estimation-a.tldr: Under anisotropic smoothness assumptions, Transformers can learn infinite-dimensional sequence mappings while avoiding the curse of dimensionality.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning analyses require the data-generating process to mix exponentially fast, meaning its dependence on earlier states fades at that rate. They may also require knowing the mixing time to choose a training step size. These requirements can be problematic with large state spaces or sparse rewards, and an unknown mixing time makes the prescribed choice difficult to use.

Multi-level Actor-Critic addresses this in infinite-horizon problems that optimize average reward. It incorporates multilevel Monte Carlo estimators into the actor, critic, and average-reward calculations. Its parameter choices do not require oracle knowledge of mixing time, and its analysis does not assume exponentially decaying mixing behavior.

Despite these relaxed requirements, MAC achieves a convergence rate comparable to state-of-the-art actor-critic algorithms. Experiments on sparse-reward problems also show superior performance. The contribution links a less restrictive theoretical foundation to practical improvements in the evaluated settings, making the approach relevant to slower-mixing problems where earlier stability conditions are difficult to satisfy.
icml-2023-beyond-exponentially-fast-mixi.tldr: MAC achieves competitive actor-critic convergence without requiring exponentially fast mixing or prior knowledge of the mixing time.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model through clients whose data remain separate. When their data distributions differ, repeated local updates can pull clients toward solutions that fit their own data but deviate from the global objective. The paper argues that approaches focused mainly on aligning local and global optimization can deteriorate when this heterogeneity is high.

FedSMOO combines alignment with an explicit concern for generalization. A dynamic regularizer directs local optima toward the global objective, while a global sharpness-aware minimization procedure seeks consistent flat minima. The two components address related goals: keeping clients oriented toward the shared problem and shaping the kinds of solutions that training reaches.

The theoretical analysis gives an O(1/T) convergence rate and a low generalization bound. Numerical studies on real-world data report strong efficiency and generality. The paper's central contribution is this joint treatment of optimization consistency and generalization, supported by both analysis and experiments, rather than treating client drift as the only consideration in federated training.
icml-2023-dynamic-regularized-sharpness-.tldr: FedSMOO combines dynamic regularization and global sharpness-aware optimization to improve consistency and generalization in federated learning.

paragraphs: This paper examines the feature space available to graph neural networks: the collection of information their learned representations can draw on. Earlier studies had emphasized optimization objectives and spectral graph theory. Here, the authors separate spatial and spectral models into determined feature spaces and trainable weights, making the feature space itself accessible to matrix-based analysis.

Their theoretical finding is that repeated aggregation tends to make features linearly correlated. When this happens, shared weights or the limited dimensionality of node attributes can restrict the resulting representations. The analysis identifies a reason that repeated processing may leave a model with a constrained set of useful features.

The authors introduce feature-subspace flattening and structural principal components to expand this space. Experiments support the effectiveness of the expanded representations, show efficient convergence, and report inference time comparable to the baseline. The findings connect a specific representational restriction with architectural remedies, suggesting that improving what features are available can benefit graph learning without a substantial inference-time increase in the reported comparisons.
icml-2023-feature-expansion-for-graph-ne.tldr: Analyzing and expanding graph neural networks' feature spaces improves representations while retaining comparable inference time in experiments.

paragraphs: When people or organizations contribute data to a shared model, they may also use the resulting service. This creates a two-way exchange: data contributors help build the model and receive benefits from its predictions. The paper studies how to describe and measure the relationship between these two sides, using settings such as recommendation, health prediction, and pooled enterprise data as motivation.

The proposed framework calls contributions outflows and benefits inflows. Reciprocity measures the balance between them. This framing separates the question of what an entity supplies from the question of what it receives, allowing the exchange itself to become an object of analysis rather than considering only the model's overall usefulness.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental evidence that some model classes are approximately reciprocal under certain distributional assumptions. This is a qualified finding about particular classes and distributions. The work presents a framework and initial results, with open directions remaining for understanding when pooled-data systems return benefits that approximately balance participants' contributions.
icml-2023-inflow-outflow-and-reciprocity.tldr: A framework measures data contributions, received benefits, and their balance, showing approximate reciprocity for some models under distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that explains expert demonstrations. Traditional approaches repeatedly solve reinforcement-learning problems as part of this process, making imitation computationally expensive. The paper questions this arrangement because learning to imitate is being handled through repeated calls to the harder problem of discovering good behavior through reinforcement learning.

The authors use additional information already connected to the expert: the distribution of states the expert visits. Their reduction uses this distribution to alleviate the global-exploration component of the reinforcement-learning subroutine. This builds on the observation that knowing where a strong policy spends time can substantially reduce the effort needed to solve a learning problem.

The resulting approach provides an exponential speedup in the theoretical analysis. Experiments on continuous-control tasks also show substantial speedups over prior methods. The key idea is that expert demonstrations can inform where learning should focus, as well as which behavior should be explained, reducing the computational burden of the imitation-learning procedure.
icml-2023-inverse-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Using the expert's state distribution reduces exploration costs in inverse reinforcement learning, yielding theoretical and practical speedups.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a Gaussian mixture when only samples inside a set S are visible. The underlying distribution combines several one-dimensional Gaussian components, but censoring determines which observations reach the learner. The task is to recover the component means and mixture weights from this selectively observed data.

The formal model has k components sharing a common variance. Its weights describe how much each component contributes, while its means describe their locations. Recovering these quantities addresses the underlying mixture, rather than simply describing the distribution of the observations that pass the censoring rule. The stated learning targets are the weights and means.

The authors propose an algorithm requiring 1/ε^{O(k)} samples to estimate those targets within ε error. This provides a finite-sample guarantee for a latent-variable model under censoring, an area where such guarantees had been missing even for simple models. The bound makes the dependence on accuracy and component count explicit: the exponent depends on k, so the guarantee should be read with that dependence in view.
icml-2023-learning-mixtures-of-gaussians.tldr: An algorithm learns the means and weights of censored univariate Gaussian mixtures with a finite-sample accuracy guarantee.

paragraphs: Neural PDE solvers approximate physical simulations, but their behavior must adapt when the parameters governing the equations change. The paper identifies limited parameter adaptation as a reason existing models struggle with PDE parameters absent from training. It proposes a component that makes those parameters an explicit guide to the model's processing.

Channel Attention guided by PDE Parameter Embeddings, or CAPE, uses parameter embeddings to guide channel attention in a neural solver. The component is designed to combine with any neural PDE solver. The authors also introduce a curriculum that gradually moves training from teacher forcing toward fully autoregressive operation, connecting training with the model's use of its own predictions.

On a PDE benchmark, CAPE combined with the curriculum produces consistent, significant improvements over baseline models. Experiments also show improved generalization to unseen PDE parameters without large increases in inference time or parameter count. The results support parameter-guided adaptation as a practical way to improve neural surrogates while keeping their additional computational burden modest.
icml-2023-learning-neural-pde-solvers-wi.tldr: CAPE guides neural PDE solvers with equation parameters, improving generalization to unseen parameters with modest additional overhead.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn a policy that chooses among discrete treatments using observational data. The aim is prescriptive: the model should select a treatment for an input. The proposed P-ReLU network uses a piecewise-linear architecture to combine strong treatment-selection performance with a form that can be interpreted.

The authors prove that the network divides the input space into disjoint polyhedral regions, with every input in a region receiving the same treatment. They also show that it can be converted into an equivalent prescriptive tree whose decisions use hyperplane splits. This provides a tree-based explanation of the trained network's treatment assignments.

Constraints can be incorporated through small architectural modifications, allowing the same approach to address constrained and unconstrained decisions. Experiments report better prescriptive accuracy than competing benchmarks. The paper also presents trees extracted from trained networks on real-world data in both scenarios. Together, the results connect flexible neural policy learning with an explicit representation of how treatment decisions divide the input space.
icml-2023-learning-prescriptive-relu-net.tldr: P-ReLU learns treatment-selection policies that support constraints and can be converted into equivalent interpretable decision trees.

paragraphs: MABe22 is a benchmark for evaluating what machine-learned representations capture about animal behavior. It brings together video and movement trajectories from biological experiments involving interacting mice, beetles and ants, and groups of flies. These settings broaden evaluation beyond the human-action datasets commonly used to develop behavior-learning methods.

The data include 4.7 million mouse frames with video and pose tracking, another 10 million mouse frames with pose alone, 10 million beetle–ant video frames, and 4.4 million fly pose frames. Accompanying analysis tasks test whether learned representations retain information about behavior and experimental conditions, including strain, time of day, and optogenetic stimulation.

The authors evaluate several leading self-supervised methods for video and trajectory representation learning. Their results show that methods developed around human actions do not transfer fully to animal data. The benchmark therefore supplies both varied recordings and concrete ways to judge their representations, supporting comparisons grounded in the information that biological analyses need to recover.
icml-2023-mabe22-a-multi-species-multi-t.tldr: MABe22 evaluates learned animal-behavior representations across species and reveals incomplete transfer from methods developed on human actions.

paragraphs: Domain decomposition methods solve discretized partial differential equations by working with subdomains. Their effectiveness depends on parameters controlling features such as overlap and boundary conditions. Previous parameter-optimization work had largely addressed one-level methods or special cases with structured grids and regularly constructed subdomains, leaving a broader multilevel setting less explored.

The paper introduces MG-GNN, a multigrid graph neural network that learns optimized parameters for two-level domain decomposition. A new unsupervised loss provides the training objective. The approach is trained on small problems and evaluated on unstructured grids orders of magnitude larger, directly testing whether learned parameter choices remain useful as problem size increases.

The reported results show robust performance on these larger grids and better optimization performance than popular hierarchical graph-network architectures. The authors also find that the new loss is critical to the improvement. The contribution therefore combines an architecture with a training objective, demonstrating that both matter when learning parameters for numerical solvers that must work beyond training-scale problems.
icml-2023-mg-gnn-multigrid-graph-neural-.tldr: MG-GNN learns two-level domain-decomposition parameters on small problems and performs robustly on much larger unstructured grids.

paragraphs: Model-based offline reinforcement learning uses learned dynamics to generate additional experience from a fixed dataset. Errors in those dynamics can mislead policy learning, so previous methods introduce conservatism to discourage unsupported exploration. This paper examines whether uncertainty about predicted next states measures the uncertainty that matters most for learning values.

The authors identify Bellman error as the ideal uncertainty target and show that next-state uncertainty measures used by MOPO give loose bounds on it. Their MOBILE algorithm instead compares Bellman estimates across an ensemble of learned dynamics models. Disagreement among these estimates supplies an uncertainty measure used to penalize the Bellman estimation.

Empirically, this measure can be significantly closer to the true Bellman error than the alternatives compared. MOBILE also outperforms earlier offline reinforcement-learning approaches on most tasks in the D4RL and NeoRL benchmarks. The findings support assessing model uncertainty through its consequences for value estimation, with the reported advantage applying to most, rather than all, evaluated tasks.
icml-2023-model-bellman-inconsistency-fo.tldr: MOBILE uses disagreement in Bellman estimates to measure model uncertainty and improve offline reinforcement learning on most evaluated benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: SignSGD updates model weights using only the signs of stochastic gradients, reducing communication requirements. Existing convergence guarantees, however, had required growing batch sizes or particular symmetry and shape assumptions about gradient noise. Error feedback offered another route to convergence under weaker assumptions, but introduced additional communication overhead.

This paper proves that momentum can establish convergence under weaker assumptions than earlier techniques. In particular, its theory does not require bounded stochastic gradients or increasing batch sizes. These results offer theoretical support for earlier empirical observations that momentum-equipped signSGD maintains good performance with small batches, where plain signSGD can struggle.

The authors further obtain an improved convergence rate when the objective is second-order smooth. That improvement is conditional on the additional smoothness property. They also extend the analysis to majority-vote signSGD and federated learning. The overall contribution is a broader theoretical foundation for a communication-efficient optimizer, together with a sharper rate in a more structured setting.
icml-2023-momentum-ensures-convergence-o.tldr: Momentum gives signSGD convergence guarantees without bounded stochastic gradients or growing batches, with faster convergence under second-order smoothness.

paragraphs: Nested expectations involve estimating averages that themselves depend on other averages. Their computational cost can rise steeply with nesting depth. For D nestings, the paper describes standard Monte Carlo costs of at least O(ε^{-(2+D)}), and sometimes O(ε^{-2(1+D)}), to reach error ε. Existing multilevel approaches considered here addressed only one nesting.

The proposed Recursive Estimator for Arbitrary Depth, or READ, exploits the recursive structure of the problem and applies randomized multilevel Monte Carlo recursively. Under suitable assumptions, it achieves optimal O(ε^{-2}) cost for every fixed D. Keeping depth fixed is part of this statement about how cost scales with requested accuracy.

Under more general assumptions, READ attains the nearly optimal cost O(ε^{-2(1+δ)}) for any δ between zero and one-half. The estimator is also unbiased, which facilitates parallelization. These results provide accuracy-dependent cost guarantees across arbitrary fixed nesting depths, with the stronger rate tied to stronger assumptions and a slightly weaker rate available more broadly.
icml-2023-optimal-randomized-multilevel-.tldr: READ estimates nested expectations with optimal or nearly optimal accuracy-dependent cost at any fixed depth under the stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect heterogeneity asks how the average effect of a treatment varies across people or other units. Many available estimators assume that measured covariates are sufficient for conditional exchangeability, allowing a causal comparison after accounting for those variables. This paper addresses settings where relying on that assumption is implausible and proxy variables are used for causal inference.

The proposed P-learner draws motivation from the R-learner and DR-learner. Its main construction is a tailored two-stage loss function for learning heterogeneous effects in the proxy-based setting. Because the estimator is expressed through loss minimization, it can be implemented with off-the-shelf machine-learning methods rather than requiring a single specialized prediction architecture.

For kernel regression, the authors establish an oracle bound on estimation error, provided the nuisance components are estimated reasonably well. This condition connects the final effect estimate to the quality of supporting estimates. The contribution is therefore both a flexible learning formulation and a conditional theoretical guarantee for one implementation, extending treatment-effect learning to a setting motivated by inadequate observed covariates.
icml-2023-proximal-causal-learning-of-co.tldr: The P-learner uses proxy variables and a two-stage loss to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects when observed-covariate exchangeability is implausible.

paragraphs: Unpaired image-to-image translation changes images between domains without paired training examples. Score-based diffusion methods have shown promise, but the paper identifies a difficulty in explicitly describing the intermediate distributions affected during generation. SDDM addresses this by organizing the generation process on manifolds so that the intertwined distributions can be optimized explicitly.

The method derives manifolds that separate distributions at adjacent time steps. It then splits the score function or energy guidance into denoising and content-refinement parts. Equalizing the refinement components allows multiple objectives to be optimized on a manifold while keeping refinement at the same noise level, giving these two roles a more explicit mathematical treatment.

SDDM also uses block adaptive instance normalization to construct lower-dimensional manifolds concentrated around the perturbed reference image. On several image-translation benchmarks, it outperforms existing score-based diffusion methods while using substantially fewer diffusion steps. The findings support separating denoising from content refinement as a way to improve both translation results and the number of generation steps required.
icml-2023-sddm-score-decomposed-diffusio.tldr: SDDM separates denoising and content refinement on manifolds, improving unpaired image translation with fewer diffusion steps.

paragraphs: Graph embedding represents vertices through locations whose distances reflect graph structure. Experiments have shown advantages for non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic representations of hierarchical graphs. Yet earlier generalization bounds were so large that they offered weak guarantees at practical data sizes, leaving a gap between empirical success and theoretical support.

This paper derives a new bound using local Rademacher complexity, treating the model as a collection of distance functions between representation pairs. The resulting dependence on the space's geometric radius R is polynomial, whereas earlier bounds could depend exponentially on R. Its fastest training-data dependence is O(1/S), compared with the earlier fastest O(1/√S).

These are improved upper bounds on generalization error, showing that previous analyses could substantially overstate the error permitted by theory. Calculations for example cases further indicate that non-Euclidean embeddings can outperform Euclidean ones with much less training data than older bounds suggested. The result strengthens theoretical support for these geometries without asserting that they win for every graph.
icml-2023-tight-and-fast-generalization-.tldr: Tighter generalization bounds give stronger theoretical support for non-Euclidean graph embeddings at practical training-data sizes.

paragraphs: A computer-vision model can learn to imitate example outputs while still producing predictions poorly aligned with how it will be used. The paper focuses on this mismatch, especially for tasks with complex structured outputs. In those settings, designing a training procedure that captures the intended use becomes more difficult.

The authors adopt a reinforcement-learning approach used in natural-language processing: tuning a pretrained model against a task reward. The starting models have already learned to imitate examples. Reward-based tuning adds an objective tied to the task, creating a direct mechanism for improving alignment between predictions and the purpose they are meant to serve.

The paper demonstrates improvements across object detection, panoptic segmentation, colorization, and image captioning. This range is the main evidence for the approach's usefulness beyond a single vision problem. The authors suggest that task-reward tuning could be broadly useful for computer vision, while the demonstrated finding is its effectiveness across the particular tasks they study.
icml-2023-tuning-computer-vision-models-.tldr: Reinforcement-learning-based task-reward tuning improves pretrained models across several computer-vision tasks.

paragraphs: A molecular graph describes connectivity, but molecular properties depend heavily on three-dimensional geometry. At room temperature, a molecule can occupy many conformations, distributed according to its Boltzmann distribution. Because many properties are averages over this distribution, accurate sampling requires capturing the variability of geometries as well as locating prominent conformations.

VonMisesNet targets that variability through rotatable bonds, which account for much of the variation in molecular shape. The graph neural network constructs a variational approximation of bond torsion angles using mixtures of von Mises distributions. Modeling these angles provides a way to generate varied conformations through the rotations that drive much of their diversity.

The authors demonstrate generation for arbitrary molecules with physical accuracy relative to the Boltzmann distribution and speeds orders of magnitude above existing sampling methods. The contribution focuses on producing distributionally meaningful samples, addressing a different goal from finding modes alone. This matters for property calculations whose accuracy depends on how the full range of conformations is represented.
icml-2023-von-mises-mixture-distribution.tldr: VonMisesNet models rotatable-bond angles to rapidly generate molecular conformations that accurately reflect Boltzmann-distributed variability.

paragraphs: Novel class discovery uses a labeled dataset of known categories to help identify previously unseen categories in unlabeled data. The paper asks when that prior knowledge helps and how the benefit can be understood formally. Its contribution is an analytical framework for a task whose practical importance had outpaced its theoretical foundations.

The authors introduce a graph representation tailored to novel class discovery and a training objective called NCD Spectral Contrastive Loss. Minimizing this loss is equivalent to factorizing the graph's adjacency matrix. That equivalence connects representation learning to a mathematical object that can be analyzed to obtain an error bound and a necessary-and-sufficient condition for discovery within the framework.

Experiments show that NSCL can match or outperform several strong baselines on common benchmark datasets. The result combines a practically competitive learning objective with an explanation of when known-class information supports the discovery task. Its theoretical conditions and error bound provide a structured account of that transfer, alongside the empirical comparisons.
icml-2023-when-and-how-does-known-class-.tldr: A spectral graph framework explains when known classes help discover novel ones and yields a theoretically supported, competitive learning objective.

paragraphs: Personalizing predictions with categorical group attributes can seem like a way to make a model more useful to each group. This paper shows that providing such information can instead lead to unnecessarily inaccurate predictions for some groups. The concern is whether each participating group actually benefits from the use of its characteristics.

The authors formalize conditions for fair use of group attributes and describe a way to check them by training one additional model. They also characterize how ordinary model-development practices can violate these conditions. This turns the broad expectation that personalization should help into requirements that can be evaluated in a prediction task.

Studies of clinical prediction tasks find that personalization often fails to provide a tailored performance improvement for every group reporting personal data. The result does not say that personalization always harms performance; it shows why its benefits need group-level scrutiny. The authors emphasize checking fair use when attributes are protected, sensitive, self-reported, or costly to obtain.
icml-2023-when-personalization-harms-per.tldr: Personalization can harm some groups, and formal fair-use checks assess whether sharing group attributes actually improves their predictions.
